Market-makers (Pinnacle, Circa, Bookmaker/CRIS, and a few sport-specific specialists) open at low limits, take respected action, and reprice. Unabated describes that as paying customers for a better number: open, get bet, move, raise limits. Retail and most offshore screens do not independently discover price. They watch the originators and move on the screen, often without taking the bet that caused the originator to move. Walters calls that the ripple effect, and names Circa, CRIS, and Pinnacle as the books other desks actually follow.

That architecture creates three different moves that look identical on a steam alert:

- **Liability shade.** One book is heavy on one side and moves to attract the other. Probability did not change. Copycat books can still echo it.
- **Information adjustment.** New information (injury, practice DNP, weather, or a max bet from an account the desk trusts) changes the desk’s number. Inventory is secondary.
- **Phony / head fake.** A respected account bets the side it does not want, in order to drag followers onto a worse number, then comes back the other way larger once limits are up.

Captain Jack’s public line is that there is no single sharp oracle anymore. Which book is the leading signal depends on the league, time to live, liquidity, and who is on the desk. Treating 2000s Pinnacle as sharp in every market is, in his words, the first mistake.

## 1. True information steam vs head-fake steam

**What true information steam looks like in the primary sources**

Real steam is fast, broad, and expensive. It starts where limits are high enough that the bet cost real money: coordinated hits at Pinnacle, Circa, Bookmaker, and peers, often through multiple accounts in the same minute. Soft books follow in seconds to a few minutes because they are copying, not because they independently received the same information. Three filters keep showing up across the desk literature:

- **Origin.** A move that starts at a high-limit market-maker and is confirmed at a second one is information. A move that starts at a low-limit screen book and only later appears at Circa or Pinnacle is usually an echo, a balancing shade, or bait.
- **Depth and agreement.** Related markets move together. Spread, moneyline, and total (or the first-half and the full-game total) should not disagree if the news is real. A half-point tick at one soft book with no key-number cross and no sibling-market confirmation is not steam.
- **Hold.** Information moves tend to stick, or keep going once the news is public. A snap-back within minutes, especially once limits rise, is the classic footprint of a phony or of one book correcting its own error.

Unannounced injury, practice DNP, and weather shifts are the cleanest information case. The market often moves before the public wire because a syndicate’s injury network or a weather model hit the originator first. Spanky’s public description of his own shop is exactly that: an injury network plus an odds screen, and the edge is beating the close, not narrating the side. By the time a retail steam alert fires, the originating size is usually already down. Published latency sketches put sharp execution at T+0 to about 90 seconds, retail copy at 2–3 minutes, and consumer alerts several minutes after that. Chasing the alert is betting the post-move price.

**What a head fake actually is, from the people who did them**

Walters’s term was “phonies.” ESPN’s reporting and his 2024 Review-Journal interview are the cleanest primary accounts, and they do not match the retail folklore one-for-one.

The mechanism he describes: bet a followed book the wrong way, small relative to the real bet, so that book moves and everyone copying it moves on air. Then, inside about a minute, hit the other side everywhere at the new number, at five to ten times the bait. If you cannot get at least five times as much down on the real side, he says there is no value in the fake. The point is almost never “I know the winner.” It is buying a key number cheaper than the book’s posted buy-points price. His example: moving 6.5 to 7, or 2.5 to 3, is “a mountain.” Fair price to buy the 3, in his telling, is about 22 cents. A wrong-side bet that drags the market onto 3, followed by a much larger bet at −110, is buying the 3 for roughly a penny.

He is explicit about where a phony is rational and where it is not. It only makes sense around 3 or 7, and maybe 6, 10, or 14. Moving 2 to 2.5, or 1 to 1.5, or any other dead number, is pointless. Super Bowl liquidity makes the trick nearly impossible. He also used wrong-side bets as cheese for partners and books that tailed him, so the visible ticket was not the position.

The ESPN WNBA All-Star case is the modern textbook, and it is a total, not a spread. Circa opened 248. A syndicate that thought the number was 30 points high had a respected account bet the over. Circa went to 252. Copiers posted around 250. The syndicate then hammered the under. The total traded as low as 191 and closed 197. Final was 93–85. A syndicate member told ESPN this was a perfect storm, not the normal case. Spanky, quoted in the same piece, said the notorious risk in reading these is getting caught with your pants down, and named Walters. Shane Sigsbee of ImawhaleSports told ESPN the decision window is on the order of 45 seconds, and that other syndicates get faked too. @TheHammerHQ has carried Circa traders on the record about spotting accounts trying to head-fake the open.

**Where your screen-book pattern fits, and where it doesn’t**

The pattern you described — hit low-limit screen books at −2.5 or −3 to trigger automated copycats, then hammer +3.5 at max on the crisp books — is a real modern variant in secondary writeups, but it is not what Walters and the ESPN sources say works. Their condition is the opposite: the bait has to land at a book other books follow. A low-limit screen move that Circa and Pinnacle ignore does not create a ripple. What does work, in the primary accounts, is:

- Bait at the originator while limits are still small (overnight college, thin totals, early opens).
- Let copiers move on air.
- Come back the other side larger once limits are up, and only if the new number has crossed 3, 7, or another real key number.

Bookmakers know the trick. Circa and peers watch which accounts move them and whether the move is one-way or a round trip. Public evidence on how often a specific retail head fake succeeds is thin. ESPN’s syndicate source said it usually does not work. Several sharp-money explainers now list “originated at a soft book, staggered, reverses once limits rise” as the tell for fake steam, and “uniform, through a key number, started at Pinnacle/Circa/CRIS, holds” as the tell for information. That is the operational distinction. A steam alert with no originator, no key-number cross, and no sibling-market confirmation is not a signal.

## 2. Key-number gamma around 3, 7, 6, 10, 4, 14

The literature does not use the word gamma. The object is the same: win probability is not linear in the spread. Most of the curvature sits on a few margins, so a half-point is a derivative, not a cosmetic hook.

Long samples (nflverse-style logs of roughly 7,000 games from 1999 through the mid-2020s, and a separate ~7,000-game regular-season cut) put the margin distribution in a stable order:

- **3** is about 15 percent of games, and it barely moves across eras (about 15.3 percent in 1999–2014, 14.5–14.7 percent in the middle windows, still about 15 percent recently). Conditioning on a close close makes it heavier: when the spread finishes between 2.5 and 3.5, the game lands on exactly 3 about 17 percent of the time. When it closes exactly on 3, the push rate is about 9 percent.
- **7** is second, roughly 9 percent over the full sample, but it is the unstable one. It ran near 9.4–9.9 percent in earlier windows, dipped to about 7.3 percent in 2020–2024 in one study, and rebounded near 9.6 percent in a completed recent season. Push rate when the close is exactly 7 is about 6.5 percent.
- **6, 10, 4, 14** are the second tier, each roughly 4.5–6 percent. 10 is a touchdown plus a field goal. 14 is two touchdowns. 6 is two field goals, or a touchdown with a failed extra point. 4 is a composite (failed two-point plus a field goal, or similar), not a base scoring unit.

That is why books hold 3 and change the price (−3 −110 becomes −3 −120) before they cross to −3.5. A move from −5.5 to −6 is mostly noise. A move from −2.5 to −3.5 is a different bet.

**Push-to-win vs loss-to-push**

These are not the same derivative, and books price them differently.

- −3 to −2.5 turns a push into a win on the most common margin. That is the expensive side. Working ranges in the buying-points literature are often 20–25 cents through 3 in ordinary games, more in low totals, and Walters’s “fair” figure for buying the 3 is about 22 cents.
- −3.5 to −3 turns a loss into a push. Valuable, cheaper than the push-to-win conversion, and still worth shopping.
- Through 7 the same logic applies at a discount: roughly 12–18 cents in the rule-of-thumb tables, because 7 is less frequent than 3.
- Through 6 or 10, about 5–10 cents, matchup-dependent. Through 14, less still. Through 5, 8, 9, or 11, almost never worth a posted premium.

The “gamma” is highest exactly on 3, next on 7, and then on 6 and 10. Away from those spikes the distribution is nearly flat, so a half-point has almost no convexity.

**What modern 4th-down and 2-point charts actually did to the distribution**

They did not dethrone 3. Field goals are still 3, and close games still end on a kick. Three’s share has been inside a tight band for 25 years.

They did dent 7 and fatten its neighbors. Extra-point distance was moved back in 2015, and two-point attempts rose. In the nflverse-style cut, 7 fell from about 9.9 percent (1999–2004) toward about 8.1 percent in 2023–2025, while 6 rose from about 4.9 percent to about 6.4 percent and 8 from about 3.2 percent to about 4.0 percent. A separate play-by-play note: from 2015 through 2025, games decided by exactly 8 included a two-point attempt far more often than other games (about 49 percent vs about 34 percent). Eight is now a real, if still secondary, margin: touchdown plus a successful two-point, or a one-score game bent by a late decision.

Rufus Peabody’s public 2-point math is the decision-chart version of the same point. With a PAT near certainty and a two-point try near 50 percent, going for two when down 14 after a score can raise win probability versus kicking twice and playing for overtime, because the success/failure tree is not symmetric. ESPN-style charts treat the PAT and the two-point as nearly equal in expected points (PAT around the mid-90s percent, two-point around the high 40s, worth double), so coaches should be choosing, not defaulting. Aggressive 4th-down charts do the same thing one level up: more go-for-it in plus territory means fewer automatic field goals and punts, which nudges some margins off 3 and onto 6, 7, or 8 depending on whether the conversion and the following score land. The empirical result so far is a fatter 6 and 8, a wobbling 7, and a 3 that refuses to die.

For pricing, the practical update is: do not pay 2010 prices for the 7 as if it were still a pure touchdown number, and do not ignore 6. Still do not pay dead-number prices to cross 5 or 9. Walters’s constraint still holds. A phony, a buy, or a middle is only rational if it captures 3, 7, or a now-livelier 6 or 10. A half-point between dead numbers is not gamma. It is juice.

## 3. Stale main lines vs lagging derivatives

Main markets and derivative markets are not the same risk system. Full-game spread, total, and moneyline sit on the primary engine, which is watched by sharps and by every copier. First-half totals, team totals, kicker points, and RB/WR yardage ladders are often on a slower model, a manual trader, or a prop desk that does not reprice in lockstep when the main total moves 2 or 2.5 points on wind or an injury.

The timing ranges in the public material, not a single measured constant:

- Sharp originators reprice a star injury or a material weather update in seconds to a couple of minutes. Automated injury-to-price pipelines are described in the 30–180 second range. A manual desk can still be at 10–30 minutes.
- US retail main lines typically follow inside a few minutes on a nationally bet game. NFL Sunday early windows are slower than primetime. One odds-comparison note puts NFL early-slate stale main lines at roughly 2–5 minutes, primetime under 2.
- Prop and alternate ripples are the lag. NBA writeups put teammate and matchup prop adjustments at 15–45 minutes after a star designation, with the spread and total already settled. Lesser-monitored players lag the stars. NFL kicker, first-half, and yardage ladders are the same structural gap: the total can be 2.5 points lower on a wind or inactive update while the derivative board is still the old number.
- Your 4–15 minute band is inside that published range for derivatives after a main-line news move. It is too slow for a Pinnacle main-line tick, and too fast to assume every prop desk. The edge, when it exists, is the gap between a moved sharp total and a derivative that has not been recast, not the side of the total itself.

Spanky’s top-down description is the syndicate version of the same trade. He is not asking who wins. He is asking which book is still showing yesterday’s price after a sharp book and a limit change have already spoken. Unabated’s line is the institutional version: a sport-weighted, vig-free blend of the market-makers that actually reach the close, used as a fair value so a slow book’s leftover price can be scored as stale rather than as a “pick.” Captain Jack’s addition is that the weights are not static. A book can be the sharp signal on Tuesday and a follower by Saturday afternoon. Time to live matters. So does which trader is on.

Two failure modes eat this trade. Ghost lines: the scanner is 10–15 seconds behind the book, so the “stale” price is already gone when the bet lands. And account death: books that welcome the first stale-line bet limit the account that keeps taking them. The market-maker side of the interaction is the opposite trade. They want the information in the main line immediately, and they accept that a slow prop desk is an invitation until the model cascade catches up. Sharps who only move the main total, and leave the kicker and the yardage ladder alone, are leaving the second leg of the same information on the table. Sharps who hit both are why the lag has compressed on star props and why it still exists on the thin rungs.

## What the named people actually add

- **Walters:** phonies exist to buy a key number cheaper than 20-plus cents, only at a followed book, only if the return bet is five to ten times larger, and never on a dead number. The Don Best / odds-screen era made the ripple mechanical.
- **Spanky:** the durable edge he describes is top-down — injury speed, odds-screen latency, middling and steam-chasing the slow book — and he treats head-fake reading as a way to get run over. Getting the bet down is harder than finding the number.
- **Captain Jack / Unabated:** market-making is sport-specific. Circa, Bookmaker, and Pinnacle are a blend, not a hierarchy. Being a market-maker means knowing when you are being head-faked. Fair value is a weighted close, not one logo.
- **Rufus Peabody:** the 2-point and 4th-down charts are win-probability problems with asymmetric trees. That is the mechanism behind 6 and 8 gaining share on 7, not a reason to stop respecting 3.
- **PlusEVAnalytics:** the public feed is pricing and de-vig technique (power method, correlated parlays), not a steam-tape. Useful as a reminder that a “fair” derivative price is a distribution, not the main line plus a flat correlation.
- **Hammer:** the useful on-record piece is the Circa side of the table — how a market-maker sets the open and how it tries to spot the account that is betting the open in order to move everyone else.

The interaction, stripped of folklore: originators sell price discovery and try not to be the mouse. Syndicates buy that discovery when it is real, and occasionally rent the copiers’ reflex when a key number is one half-point away and the return bet will be much larger. Everyone else is watching a screen that cannot tell those two apart unless it shows who moved first, whether a key number was crossed, whether the sibling markets agreed, and whether the move held after limits came up.

waves.title: Cross-Player Zero-Sum Simplex Conservation & Asymmetric Tail Dependence in Same-Game Parlays
waves.content:
**The core mathematical flaws in retail sportsbook and public player-prop/SGP modeling stem from treating outcomes as (nearly) independent marginals or using simplistic elliptical dependence structures.** This ignores the constrained, compositional nature of football statistics (zero-sum allocation of snaps, targets, carries, air yards, and touchdowns within a team’s fixed opportunities) and the strong asymmetric tail dependence induced by game script, pace, and variance in volume. Quantitative research in sports analytics, optimal transport (OT), compositional data modeling, DFS/portfolio optimization, and copula-based risk/pricing highlights these issues. Empirical measurements (e.g., QB passing yards and WR1 receiving yards occurring together ~1.35× more often than independence) and pricing discussions confirm mispricing in correlated SGPs.[[1]](https://www.etparlays.com/nfl-prop-correlation-index)[[2]](https://bettorsearch.com/correlation-that-costs-pricing-parlays-and-same-game-props-with-copulas/)[[3]](https://wizardofodds.com/article/same-game-parlays-the-mathematics-of-correlation/)

Twitter/X quant and modeling discussions echo that combo/SGP pricing leaves edge when legs are treated as independent despite shared game-script drivers; sophisticated models of correlation capture this, while books’ correlation adjustments are often insufficient or opaque.[[4]](https://x.com/polytutor/status/2117214738841010436)

### (1) Zero-Sum Simplex Conservation Violation
Retail and many public models generate marginal distributions for each player prop (e.g., receptions ~ NegativeBinomial or Poisson; yards ~ skewed normal, gamma, or lognormal; TDs ~ Poisson or zero-inflated) and price SGPs by multiplying adjusted probabilities or running independent Monte Carlo draws. Summing the implied medians (or means) across a team’s pass-catchers, rushers, or scorers frequently deviates from the team’s implied total (derived from game total, spread, and pace). This occurs because:

- Medians of right-skewed, zero-inflated distributions (common for secondary WRs, backup RBs, or low-usage TEs) lie below the means. Sum of medians therefore undershoots the expected team total (E[∑Y_i] ≈ team implied).
- High-usage players’ overs can be offset by zeros elsewhere, but independent modeling does not enforce non-negativity + exact summation constraints.
- Game outcomes (pass attempts, carries, snaps) are fixed in a given realization; independent marginals allow “impossible” joint realizations (e.g., every WR exceeding their expected share simultaneously while team total is fixed low).[[5]](https://unabated.com/post/the-biggest-mistake-youre-making-when-betting-nfl-player-props)

Target-share and usage metrics partially mitigate this (project player stat = team volume projection × share × efficiency), but marginal prop setting still violates joint conservation. Empirical work on target share emphasizes it as a proportion of fixed team attempts, yet full joint simulation rarely projects onto the simplex.[[6]](https://atswins.ai/articles/recent-articles/nfl-player-props-based-on-target-share-betting-strategy-guide/)[[7]](https://www.propsedge.io/blog/nfl-player-props-guide)

**Dirichlet distribution enforces exact conservation for shares.** Model the vector of target shares, carry shares, snap shares, or air-yard shares **s = (s₁, …, sₖ)** (sᵢ ≥ 0, ∑sᵢ = 1) as:

\[
\mathbf{s} \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}), \quad f(\mathbf{s} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{1}{B(\boldsymbol{\alpha})} \prod_{i=1}^k s_i^{\alpha_i - 1}, \quad B(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{\prod \Gamma(\alpha_i)}{\Gamma(\sum \alpha_i)}
\]

Given team-level volume *T* (attempts, carries, or snaps, drawn from its own marginal), the allocation is exactly conserved: targets/caries_i = s_i × *T* (or Multinomial(*T*; **s**) for discrete counts). Marginal for player *i* is Beta(α_i, ∑_{j≠i} α_j). This is used in DFS lineup modeling via Dirichlet-multinomial for opponent portfolio simulation and extends naturally to props.[[8]](https://www.columbia.edu/~mh2078/DFS_Revision_1_May2019.pdf)[[8]](https://www.columbia.edu/~mh2078/DFS_Revision_1_May2019.pdf)

For continuous yards or more flexible marginals that must still sum exactly to a team total (or match multiple marginals simultaneously), **entropic optimal transport with Sinkhorn-Knopp scaling** projects independent player marginals μ₁, …, μₖ onto the constraint that ∑ player outcomes = team realization (or matches a team histogram ν). The entropic OT problem is:

\[
\min_{\pi \in \Pi(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \nu)} \langle C, \pi \rangle - \varepsilon H(\pi)
\]

subject to marginal constraints (Π denotes couplings with prescribed marginals). This is solved iteratively via Sinkhorn-Knopp: initialize kernel *K_{ij} = exp(-C_{ij}/ε)*; alternately scale row and column factors **u**, **v** so that the coupling π = diag(**u**) *K* diag(**v**) matches the target marginal vectors **a**, **b** (player histograms and team total histogram). The result yields simulations or barycentric weights that exactly conserve snaps/targets/carries/air yards/TDs while staying closest (in regularized Wasserstein distance) to the independent marginal predictions. Unbalanced variants handle mass discrepancies (e.g., injuries, garbage time). Recent sports analytics applies this to regress player histograms onto team distributions and cluster styles via Wasserstein barycenters.[[9]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01388-7)[[9]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40537-026-01388-7)

Retail/public models violate this simplex constraint; advanced simulators using Dirichlet + OT/Sinkhorn produce internally consistent joint samples for SGP pricing and avoid arbitrage against team totals.

### (2) Asymmetric Tail Dependence (Clayton/Gumbel/Vine vs. Gaussian Copula)
Even when marginals are reasonable and simple correlations are applied, Gaussian copulas (or independence) drastically underprice joint tail events in SGPs. Football outcomes exhibit strong *asymmetric* dependence driven by game script: high-total shootouts inflate multiple passing props together (upper-tail clustering); trench warfare, blowouts, or script-driven run-heavy/favorite-led games cluster high carries for the favored RB, high pass attempts for the trailing QB, and defensive opportunities (e.g., sacks) in ways that produce lower-tail or mixed dependence.[[2]](https://bettorsearch.com/correlation-that-costs-pricing-parlays-and-same-game-props-with-copulas/)[[3]](https://wizardofodds.com/article/same-game-parlays-the-mathematics-of-correlation/)

The **Gaussian copula** is:

\[
C_G(\mathbf{u}; R) = \Phi_R(\Phi^{-1}(u_1), \dots, \Phi^{-1}(u_d))
\]

where Φ_R is the multivariate standard normal CDF with correlation matrix *R*, and Φ^{-1} is the univariate normal inverse CDF. It preserves arbitrary marginals while imposing elliptical/symmetric dependence. Critically, its tail dependence coefficients are zero:

\[
\lambda_U = \lambda_L = 0 \quad (\text{for } |\rho_{ij}| < 1)
\]

Thus P(U₁ > 1−q, …, U_d > 1−q) decays too quickly as q → 0. It underestimates the probability of extreme upper-tail shootouts (e.g., QB 300+ pass yds ∩ WR1 100+ rec yds ∩ secondary WR 90+ rec yds) and corresponding lower-tail or script-driven trench events (Favorite RB 22+ carries ∩ Underdog QB 38+ pass attempts ∩ Favorite Edge 1+ sack). Empirical correlations (QB pass yds × WR1 rec yds ≈ 1.35× independent) already show positive dependence; tails amplify this further.[[1]](https://www.etparlays.com/nfl-prop-correlation-index)

**Archimedean copulas capture asymmetry.** Clayton (lower-tail emphasis):

\[
C_C(u,v;\theta) = \max\left( (u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1)^{-1/\theta}, 0 \right), \quad \theta > 0
\]

has lower tail dependence λ_L = 2^{−1/θ} > 0, λ_U = 0.

Gumbel (upper-tail emphasis):

\[
C_G(u,v;\theta) = \exp\left( -[ (-\ln u)^\theta + (-\ln v)^\theta ]^{1/\theta} \right), \quad \theta \geq 1
\]

has upper tail dependence λ_U = 2 − 2^{1/θ} > 0, λ_L = 0.

Student-t has symmetric tail dependence (both tails) but still lacks the flexibility to mix directions across variable pairs.[[10]](https://www.rajivgopinath.com/blogs/statistics-and-data-science-hub/types-of-copulas)[[11]](https://metricgate.com/blogs/copula-dependency-modeling-basics/)

**Vine copulas** (pair-copula constructions, C-vine or D-vine) allow each bivariate conditional pair to select its own family (Clayton on some edges for crash-like lower tails, Gumbel on others for boom-like upper tails, Gaussian/Frank in the center). This flexibly models the heterogeneous asymmetric dependence in football without assuming a single global structure. Hierarchical or mixture copulas provide further options. Research on risk, insurance, and pairs trading consistently shows Gaussian (and even t-) copulas misprice tail probabilities relative to vines or asymmetric Archimedean families; the 2008 CDO crisis is the canonical warning for Gaussian copula underestimation of joint extremes.[[12]](https://hudsonthames.org/copula-for-pairs-trading-introduction/)[[13]](https://metricgate.com/docs/copula-vine-pair/)

In SGP pricing, books often rely on Gaussian copulas (or correlation matrices with Gaussian inversion) plus empirical overrides because they are computationally tractable in moderate-to-high dimensions. This systematically underprices the correlated tail SGPs described (upper-tail passing explosions and lower/script-driven trench clusters), creating +EV opportunities for models using Dirichlet-simulated marginals projected via Sinkhorn OT and vine copulas calibrated to historical game-script clusters.[[3]](https://wizardofodds.com/article/same-game-parlays-the-mathematics-of-correlation/)

These flaws—non-conservation of team-level zerosum quantities and Gaussian’s inability to capture asymmetric tail dependence—are among the deepest structural weaknesses. Sharp quantitative approaches (Dirichlet + Sinkhorn for conservation; vine copulas mixing Clayton/Gumbel for tails) produce internally consistent, tail-aware joint distributions that expose retail SGP mispricing, consistent with both academic sports analytics/OT work and practitioner measurement of NFL prop correlations.

waves.title: Why Standard NFL Analytics Lie: Causal Confounders in EPA, CPOE, YPRR, RYOE & PBWR
waves.content:
**Standard public NFL metrics like EPA/play, CPOE, YPRR, RYOE, PBWR, PRWR, and PROE (or similar over-expected rush/pass metrics) are valuable for describing outcomes but suffer from deep causal confounding, credit-assignment problems, selection bias, and sensitivity to scheme, context, and unmeasured dynamics.**[[1]](https://sumersports.com/the-zone/nfl-advanced-stats/)[[2]](https://www.nfeloapp.com/analysis/over-expected-explained-what-are-cpoe-ryoe-and-yacoe/)

Public play-by-play and tracking data make full isolation of individual skill nearly impossible without strong assumptions. EPA aggregates value but struggles with dividing credit among QB, OL, WR routes, RB vision, coaching play design, and luck (fumbles, tipped passes, YAC variance). CPOE and “over expected” metrics residualize against observable difficulty (air yards, separation, pressure proximity, down/distance), yet the expectation models often omit or imperfectly capture scheme features that systematically alter difficulty. Year-to-year stability is modest for many; single-season outliers frequently regress sharply.[[2]](https://www.nfeloapp.com/analysis/over-expected-explained-what-are-cpoe-ryoe-and-yacoe/)[[3]](https://www.covers.com/nfl/key-advanced-metrics-betting-tips)

Advanced research and independent analysts (Ben Baldwin/nflfastR, Brian Burke/ESPN Analytics, academic survival-analysis and causal papers) have highlighted these issues through residualization, multilevel models, survival/hazard frameworks, and propensity-style adjustments.[[4]](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33664v2)[[5]](https://arxiv.org/html/1802.00998v2) The critiques below focus on the four requested mechanisms with mathematical structure.

### (1) RPOs, screens, motion-at-snap free releases, and condensed bunch formations inflating QB CPOE/EPA and WR YPRR while masking isolated 1-on-1 boundary failure

These scheme elements systematically lower true difficulty below what observable tracking features (separation at throw, aDOT, time-to-throw) register. Completion probability models (logistic or tree-based in nflfastR/Next Gen Stats) condition on post-snap observables. If motion or bunch creates *pre-snap* or *at-snap* advantages (defenders frozen, rub/pick routes, condensed zones overwhelmed by numbers), the resulting high separation at release is credited to the QB/WR rather than the design.[[6]](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/heuristic-expectation-metrics-football-rivka-boord)

- **RPOs and screens**: The QB reads a defender; a “pass” decision often follows defensive commitment, producing high-probability quick throws or designed screens with built-in YAC. These have low variance and high completion rates. EPA credits the outcome; CPOE sees “easy” completion relative to average throws of similar aDOT/separation.
- **Motion at snap**: Creates free releases (defender must honor jet/motion or run fake), producing cleaner windows and higher target separation than static routes. This boosts both completion probability and YPRR (yards per route run).
- **Condensed bunch**: Generates rubs, natural picks, or zone overloads. Receivers gain easy yards in condensed space; boundary 1-on-1 winning on 3rd-and-7+ is avoided.

**Mathematical view**: Let CP = P(complete | air_yards, sep_at_throw, pressure_proximity, down_dist, ...). Observed CPOE = (I_complete − CP) averaged. But sep_at_throw ← scheme (motion, bunch, RPO freeze). If the CP model does not fully saturate on formation density, motion type, RPO indicator, or pre-snap defender alignment, then Cov(scheme_layup, residual) > 0. QB/WR CPOE and EPA are inflated; YPRR (yards/route) inherits the same bias because easy targets produce YAC “over expected.” On true isolated boundary routes (no motion, no rub, man coverage on 3rd-and-7+), the same QB/WR may post negative residuals, revealing inability to create or win against press/man without scheme help. This is classic omitted-variable bias or post-treatment confounding: scheme affects both the “treatment” (easy target) and the outcome metric.[[7]](https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=12032&context=etd)

Film-aware analysts note that high-CPOE QBs on heavy RPO/screen/motion offenses can look elite in aggregates while struggling when defenses take away the easy stuff. Adjusted-EPA attempts (e.g., penalizing YAC merchants, adjusting for pass pro) partially mitigate but cannot fully residualize unmeasured scheme creativity.[[8]](https://x.com/benbbaldwin/status/1876992599367589907)

### (2) QB mobility and read-option mesh-point conflict freezing backside edge defenders, inflating RB RYOE and YBC/Att despite mediocre vision

RYOE regresses rushing yards on box count, gap, down/distance, defensive front, and higher-order terms It attributes residual yards to the RB. However, dynamic elements—QB boot threat, mesh-point conflict in read-option, or designed QB mobility—hold the backside edge defender for an extra 0.35–0.60 seconds. This creates lanes or delays pursuit beyond what static pre-snap box or front variables capture.[[2]](https://www.nfeloapp.com/analysis/over-expected-explained-what-are-cpoe-ryoe-and-yacoe/)

The expectation model sees a “normal” run gap but misses the equilibrium in which the defender cannot fully commit without risking QB keep. Result: actual yards before contact (YBC/Att) and total RYOE rise even if the RB’s vision, burst, or decision-making at the second level is average. Year-to-year correlation of RYOE is near zero in small samples; only multi-year data (with selection bias) begins to stabilize, suggesting heavy scheme/OL/QB-threat confounding.[[2]](https://www.nfeloapp.com/analysis/over-expected-explained-what-are-cpoe-ryoe-and-yacoe/)

**Causal DAG**: QB_threat → defender_freeze_time → gap_persistence → yards. The RB receives credit for the downstream outcome. Multilevel or random-effects models that include QB mobility as a cluster or covariate reduce but do not eliminate this; full tracking of defender hip orientation or acceleration vectors toward mesh would be needed. Public models lack it, so RYOE partly measures “RB skill conditional on QB threat freezing edges” rather than pure vision or elusiveness.

### (3) ESPN 2.5-second PBWR/PRWR threshold fails on 3-step quick game versus 7-step play-action; hazard functions h(t) over continuous t ∈ [1.5s, 4.5s] solve it

PBWR (Pass Block Win Rate) and PRWR count a “win” for the blocker if the block is sustained until the rusher is not within a threshold distance by 2.5 seconds post-snap (or vice-versa for rusher). The 2.5 s threshold approximates average time-to-throw on conventional dropbacks and was chosen to separate known good players in early data.[[9]](https://www.cfb51.com/pub/?p=100155)[[10]](https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=26888038)

It fails across play types:
- **3-step quick game / screens**: Time-to-throw ≈ 1.8–2.3 s. Blocks need only hold briefly; a blocker who sustains until throw but is beaten at t=2.6 s is scored a “loss” despite success relative to release timing. Quick-game PBWR looks artificially low.
- **7-step play-action/deep drop**: Time-to-throw > 3.0–4.0+ s. Sustaining to 2.5 s is necessary but insufficient; late pressure at t=3.5 s can still destroy the play. PBWR over-rewards marginal long holds if release is delayed.

This is a discrete coarsening of a continuous-time process. A single threshold ignores the full survival curve and interaction with actual time-to-throw distribution. Quick-release QBs (e.g., certain West Coast or no-huddle schemes) systematically lower observed PBWR even with competent line play; slow-developing play-action inflates it. Opponent quality, stunts, double-team handoffs, and bull-rush disruption further confound the binary win/loss.[[11]](https://www.espn.com/espn/print?id=49672562)[[12]](https://wsb.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/HAFIZ_PRSS-A-new-metric.pdf)

**Hazard-function solution**: Model block sustain as a survival process. Let T = time until rusher beats blocker (or block fails). The hazard function is:

h(t) = lim_{Δt→0} [P(t ≤ T < t+Δt | T ≥ t) / Δt]

This is the instantaneous failure rate at t conditional on survival to t. The cumulative hazard H(t) = ∫_0^t h(u) du yields the survival function S(t) = exp(−H(t)) = P(T > t).

Player-specific h_i(t) (via Cox proportional hazards, frailty models, or nonparametric Nelson-Aalen with player indicators) over t ∈ [1.5s, 4.5s] captures the full curve. Expected wins can be integrated against the empirical time-to-throw distribution conditional on play type (quick game vs. play-action). This yields a continuous, time-weighted protection metric rather than a single arbitrary cutoff. It directly solves the mismatch: quick-game blocks are evaluated only in the relevant early window; long drops penalize late failures appropriately. Newer research uses probabilistic assignment of who is blocking whom (Voronoi, matching) plus hazard regression to handle stunts and exchanges.[[4]](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33664v2)[[12]](https://wsb.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/HAFIZ_PRSS-A-new-metric.pdf)

Brian Burke has noted that PBWR/PRWR are built on survival ideas; the hazard framing makes the time dependence explicit and allows conditioning on observed release time.[[13]](https://x.com/bburkeESPN/status/1485370869622919176)

### (4) Exact Frisch-Waugh-Lovell / propensity-score residualization equations to strip scheme layups from true player skill

To isolate player skill orthogonal to scheme “layups” (RPO, screen, motion, bunch, play-action rate, drop depth, and higher-order terms), use partial regression (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem) or propensity-score methods.

**Frisch-Waugh-Lovell (FWL)**: Suppose outcome metric M (EPA contribution, completion indicator, yards, block-sustain time) for play i by player j:

M_i = β Skill_j + γ′ Scheme_i + δ′ Context_i + ε_i

Scheme_i is a vector of play-type indicators or continuous features (motion rate, bunch dummy, RPO flag, time-to-throw bin, formation density, and higher-order terms).

To recover β net of scheme:

1. Regress M on Scheme (and Context): M = Π̂_Scheme + r_M  (residual r_M)
2. Regress a player-skill proxy (or player fixed effect / rating) S_j on Scheme: S = Π̂_Scheme_S + r_S
3. Regress r_M on r_S: coefficient on r_S is exactly the multivariate OLS β on Skill after controlling for Scheme.

In matrix notation, let Z = [Scheme Context], X = player indicators or skill proxy. The partial coefficient is:

β = (X′ M_Z X)^{−1} X′ M_Z M

where M_Z = I − Z(Z′Z)^{−1}Z′ is the residual-maker orthogonal to Z. This is numerically identical to full OLS but isolates the variation in skill orthogonal to scheme. Player-level aggregates of r_M become “scheme-adjusted” metrics.[[14]](https://metricgate.com/calculator/frisch-waugh-lovell)

**Propensity-score residualization**: Estimate p_i = Pr(layup_scheme_i | pre-snap covariates, personnel, game state) via logistic or GBM. Then include p_i, p_i², or 1/(1−p_i) (inverse probability weights for “against the grain” plays) in the regression above, or residualize M against a flexible function of p_i. The player residual or coefficient on player indicators now reflects performance on plays whose scheme propensity is controlled for. In potential-outcomes terms this approximates E[M(1) − M(0) | player] where “treatment” is difficult vs. easy scheme.

Multilevel models (as in nflWAR-style approaches) add partial pooling and random effects for QB-OL-WR clusters, further shrinking noisy scheme-contaminated estimates.[[5]](https://arxiv.org/html/1802.00998v2)

These techniques do not magically create unconfounded estimates—unmeasured route quality, coaching creativity, and dynamic defender reactions remain—but they systematically strip observable scheme layups, improving isolation of repeatable individual skill. Applied carefully to large samples with rich tracking, they yield more stable rankings than raw EPA/CPOE/RYOE.

In summary, these metrics describe what happened efficiently but require heavy contextual conditioning, survival modeling for protection, and explicit residualization/propensity controls to approach causal claims about player talent. Public data limitations mean the deepest “true skill” estimates still blend film, proprietary tracking, and subject-matter expertise with these statistical adjustments. The community continues refining them; hazard-based continuous metrics and richer scheme saturation in expectation models represent the frontier.

waves.title: QB Post-Hit Trauma Hysteresis, Phantom Pressure Drift & Post-Snap Disguise Processing
waves.content:
The public record supports a within-game accuracy penalty after hits, and film language about a sped-up clock and dropped eyes, but it does not support the specific biomechanical numbers in the question. Those belong in a measurement spec, not in a citation. A Hawkes (or shot-noise) hazard is a reasonable way to write the idea down. It is not a model any of the named accounts have published.

## What the numbers actually show

PFF’s Nathan Jahnke, using every regular-season and playoff passer over six seasons, found a within-game cumulative effect, not just a same-play effect. Accuracy percentage sat at 73.0% before any sack or hit in the game and fell about half a point per subsequent sack or hit. An above-average quarterback after five hits looked like an average quarterback who had taken none. After ten, he looked below average. Interception rate moved the same direction, from a 2.5% baseline with a clean game. A follow-up that held depth of target and quarter roughly fixed still showed the slope. Elite passers (Rodgers, Brees, Manning, Brady in that sample) were flatter through the first few hits. First-round rookies lost about a full accuracy point per hit, twice the league rate. [[1]](https://www.pff.com/news/cumulative-effect-hitting-the-qb) [[2]](https://www.pff.com/news/cumulative-effect-a-deeper-look) [[3]](https://www.pff.com/news/cumulative-effect-individual-qbs)

That is hysteresis of decision quality, not of the clock. The 2021 PFF resilience study (Tej Seth and Ryan Weisman) is the direct test of “he gets the ball out faster on the next snap.” Plays that produced a hit averaged 3.00 seconds to throw. The next play averaged 2.72 seconds. Ordinary plays averaged 2.71 seconds. The immediate time-to-throw shift is a rounding error. Hit rate itself is sticky year to year and survives a team change, so contact is partly a quarterback trait, not only an offensive-line trait. [[4]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-measuring-quarterback-resilience-how-each-nfl-quarterback-performs-after-getting-hit)

Same-play pressure is a different, much larger effect. Completion rate on a hit falls from the low 60s to the high 30s, and interception rate roughly doubles. Clean-pocket versus pressure grade gaps of about 30 PFF points, and large jumps in turnover-worthy plays under pressure, are the modern version of that same-snap collapse. [[1]](https://www.pff.com/news/cumulative-effect-hitting-the-qb) [[5]](https://www.pff.com/news/nfl-quarterbacks-under-pressure)

So the literature says: hits degrade later throws inside the same game, the penalty stacks, rookies take it harder, and the mechanism is not a measurable one-snap shortening of time to throw in the aggregate. If early interior hits speed the clock on later clean pockets, that signal is buried inside decision type (checkdown versus shot, eyes down versus eyes up, climb versus bail), not in mean snap-to-throw.

## Film language from the accounts you named

I did not find posts or breakdowns from @danorlovsky7, @Nate_Tice, @Kurt13Warner, @TedNguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis), @BenjaminSolak, @PattonAnalytics, or @PFF_Moo that measure drift at 110–130 degrees out of the tackle box, or checkdowns 0.3 seconds early, or that isolate A/B-gap hits and strip-sacks as a distinct hysteresis class. Those are a proposed coding scheme. What those analysts do say lines up with the mechanism, not the angles.

Dan Orlovsky, on Aaron Rodgers, described the failure mode in plain language: if the ball is not out immediately and the picture is not clean around 2.5 seconds, the eyes drop because the quarterback does not want to be hit, and the grade collapses. The prescription he offered was quick game or play-action, not more pure shotgun dropback. On Jayden Daniels he flagged the cleaner version of the same tell: eyes drop in a pocket that is still clean, and the quarterback thinks “get out,” leaving throws on the table. [[6]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dsZ_UAQDfd4) [[7]](https://www.thecoldwire.com/dan-orlovsky-names-1-potential-flaw-with-jayden-daniels/)

Kurt Warner’s version is feet-first. On Bo Nix he wrote that Nix is almost moving before he hits the top of the drop, and that fast feet mean a fast mind. His fix is to play slower and hold patience in the pocket. In the feet-to-route work he treats an early bail as lost yards even on completions: the quarterback is already leaving because the feet got ahead of the route, so a hitch and a throw on time never happen. Viewer discussion on his Bryce Young tape explicitly asks whether the regression to happy feet is distrust of the line after being hit, including a bull-rush into the knee. That is the hysteresis story in coaching language. [[8]](https://broncoswire.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/broncos/2025/11/12/broncos-kurt-warner-reacts-bo-nix-footwork/87224887007/) [[9]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ojJHk6sdnqk)

Nate Tice and Benjamin Solak talk about the opposite behavior as the skill. Tice highlights pocket movement that keeps two hands on the ball and eyes downfield, and treats leaky pockets plus stubborn progression as the sack generator. Solak’s Geno Smith clip is the cognitive counter to an underneath defender: the helmet moves Fred Warner just far enough to open the backside dig. His Caleb Williams notes separate “climb and throw” from “the pocket is clean and nothing is open, so escape.” Climbing the A-gap with eyes up is the behavior the trauma model says gets replaced, after interior contact, by a backward-lateral drift. [[10]](https://x.com/BenjaminSolak/status/1858903191523385705)

Sean Payton’s public line on Nix is the same clock problem from the sideline: a fast internal clock avoids sacks and also bails half a second before a route over the middle finishes. He treats a clock that is too fast as easier to fix than a clock that is too slow. [[11]](https://denversports.com/nfl/denver-broncos/payton-bo-nix-clock)

A usable film code, if you want to test the hypothesis the aggregate time-to-throw study missed, would mark only subsequent snaps that chart as clean (no hurry, hit, or sack) and score three binary tells: eyes leave the progression to the rush, launch point leaves the tackle box on a path that is backward and lateral rather than a climb through the A-gap, and the throw is a checkdown or throwaway inside the first hitch when the called concept still had time. The 110–130 degree band and the 0.3 second early threshold are reasonable bins for tracking data. They are not published results.

Interior A/B-gap hits and strip-sacks are the right marks to overweight, for a reason the mean studies never split. Edge pressure is in the quarterback’s spatial prior. Contact through the A or B gap, or a strip, is contact from the direction he is supposed to climb. That is the event most likely to rewrite the next clean pocket from “step up, eyes downfield” to “drift at an angle and get it out.”

## Cognitive break when the shell spins

The second failure is not trauma. It is a locked pre-snap hypothesis.

Cover 1 Robber shows two high, then one safety rotates to the deep middle and the other rolls to the low hole to cut digs, crosses, and slants. Cover 3 Buzz (and weak-rotation Cover 3) also starts two-high, then one safety buzzes to the curl/hook, the other takes the deep middle third, and the corners bail. The dig and the crosser that looked open against a two-high shell close as the buzz or robber arrives. [[12]](https://alleyesdbcamp.com/cover-1-robber-explained/) [[13]](https://mohrperformance.co/blog/what-is-cover-3-buzz) [[14]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ROliJ27Br9A)

The quarterback error is treating the pre-snap shell as the coverage. Joe Moorhead’s teaching order is the corrective: shell first (one-high or two-high) as a hypothesis that deletes part of the menu, then eyes, then a post-snap confirm or correct. Defensive coordinators say the same thing from the other side. UTSA’s Jess Loepp: do not creep before the snap. Make the quarterback solve the rotation while the ball is coming to him. Ted Nguyen’s public work is full of the same object — shells that lie until the snap, cadence and alerts that undress a static look — without a published within-game decay curve for quarterbacks who keep throwing the pre-snap answer. [[15]](https://coachandcoordinator.com/qb-pre-snap-coverage-recognition-joe-moorhead/) [[16]](https://x.com/JamesALight/status/1913251853032181860)

On film the miss looks like this. The quarterback confirms two-high, locks the dig or crosser as the answer to that shell, and delivers into the robber or the buzz player who spun at the snap. Solak’s Geno example is the counter-skill: move a second-level defender with the helmet, then throw the dig away from him. A quarterback who has already been hit tends to skip that confirm. The eyes are already coming down, so the post-snap spin is never seen, and the pre-snap indicator becomes the throw.

PFF’s middle-of-field disguise rates exist because this spin is now common enough to chart. The quarterback skill that survives it is a post-snap confirm, not a better pre-snap guess.

## A Hawkes hazard for trauma and turnover-worthy plays

Hawkes processes have been fit to sports event sequences, including AFL injuries as self-exciting cascades and marked Hawkes models of NFL play sequences. They have not been fit, in anything public, to intra-game quarterback trauma and turnover-worthy-play hazard. [[17]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42979-025-03939-w) [[18]](https://statistics.ucdavis.edu/sites/g/files/dgvnsk5166/files/inline-files/AdityaGantawarHonorsStudyReport.pdf)

Index plays by dropback number \(n = 1, \ldots, N\) inside one game, and reset the excitation at the next game. Let \(T\) be trauma events with mark \(m\) in {interior A/B hit, strip-sack, edge hit, hurry}. Let \(D\) be decision failures: turnover-worthy plays, plus the clean-pocket tells above if you code them. Covariates \(x_n\) cover down, distance, score, called drop depth, and whether the current pocket is clean.

A marked bivariate Hawkes on the dropback index:

\[
\lambda_T(n) = \mu_T(x_n) + \sum_{n_i < n} \alpha_T(m_i)\, e^{-\beta_T (n - n_i)}
\]

\[
\lambda_D(n) = \mu_D(x_n) + \sum_{n_i < n} \alpha_{D \leftarrow T}(m_i)\, e^{-\beta_{DT}(n - n_i)} + \sum_{n_j < n} \alpha_{DD}\, e^{-\beta_{DD}(n - n_j)}
\]

\(\mu_T\) is the opponent’s pressure rate given the play call. \(\mu_D\) is the quarterback’s baseline turnover-worthy-play rate on that down and drop, with a separate intercept on clean pockets. The cross kernel \(\alpha_{D \leftarrow T}(m)\) is the hysteresis. Estimate it larger for interior A/B hits and strip-sacks than for edge hurries. The own-kernel \(\alpha_{DD}\) is panic feeding panic: one early checkdown or one stare-down into a robber raises the rate of the next one.

Jahnke’s half-point-per-hit slope looks more like a slow within-game state than a one-snap spike. The 2021 timing study says a fast kernel on time-to-throw is close to zero. Fit both decays. If \(\beta_{DT}\) on time-to-throw is large and the effect on turnover-worthy plays and clean-pocket bails is small, the data match the papers: quality decays, the clock does not, in the mean. A practical alternative that matches the accuracy charts is a latent state rather than a fast exponential:

\[
S_n = \sum_{n_i < n} w(m_i)\, e^{-\beta (n - n_i)}, \qquad \lambda_D(n) = \mu_D(x_n)\, \exp(\gamma S_n)
\]

with \(w\) highest on interior hits and strip-sacks, \(\beta\) small enough that \(S_n\) barely decays before halftime, and \(\gamma\) allowed to differ for rookies versus veterans. Elite-quarterback resilience is a smaller \(\gamma\), not a different \(\mu\).

Add a second excitation for the cognitive break. Let \(R_n = 1\) when the defense spins (two-high to Cover 1 Robber, or two-high to Cover 3 Buzz). Do not put \(R\) in the trauma kernel. Put it in the decision kernel as a covariate, and let trauma raise the weight on the pre-snap lock:

\[
\lambda_D(n) = \mu_D(x_n)\, \exp\big(\gamma S_n + \delta R_n + \theta S_n R_n\big)
\]

\(\delta\) is the cost of a spin against a calm quarterback who still confirms post-snap. \(\theta\) is the interaction you care about: after interior contact, the same spin is more expensive because the eyes are already down and the post-snap confirm is skipped. That term is the joint model of the two failure modes. It is identifiable if you have tracking or charted shells, clean-pocket tags, and turnover-worthy-play grades on the same dropbacks. None of the accounts above have published that fit.

Estimate by maximum likelihood on the conditional intensities, or by treating the branching structure the way the AFL injury papers do, so each turnover-worthy play is either an immigrant (baseline) or an offspring of a prior hit. Report \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) by mark. If interior hits do not out-excite edge hits on later clean pockets, the A/B-gap story is film folklore. If they do, and time-to-throw still does not move, the hysteresis lives in eyes, launch angle, and throw choice, which is exactly where the 2021 clock study would have missed it.

waves.title: Weakest-Link Trench Topology, Adjacent OL Synergy Breakdown & Targeted Stunt Exploitation
waves.content:
**Offensive line (OL) pass protection is a non-linear, systems-level problem dominated by the weakest link in the chain and the coordination strength between adjacent pairs, not an arithmetic average of five (or six, including chips) individual grades or snap counts.**[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJgFiFd_r34)[[2]](https://trenchwarfare.substack.com/p/how-offensive-structure-shapes-ol)

Film analysts and evaluators such as Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL), Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL), Cody Alexander (@MatchQuarters), Duke Manyweather, and data-oriented voices like Sam Hoppen consistently highlight this through breakdowns of specific pressures, communication failures, and scheme exploitation. One missed assignment, poor handoff on a stunt, or broken pre-snap call collapses the pocket regardless of how well the other four linemen perform. This is why inserting a backup with limited shared reps with his neighbors produces outsized negative effects, and why elite defensive coordinators immediately probe new or injured combinations rather than waiting to “average” them out.

### (1) DCs Target a Single Backup Guard, Center, or Tackle with T-E / E-T Twists, A-Gap Mugged Linebackers, and Overload 5-0 Fronts

Coordinators including Steve Spagnuolo, Brian Flores, Mike Macdonald, Vic Fangio, Robert Saleh, and Jim Schwartz (or their schematic descendants) design pressures to create immediate post-snap confusion and late pass-off decisions between two linemen who have rarely worked together.[[3]](https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2113992313160544675)[[4]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eoo6odNngdM)[[5]](https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2023/11/22/23971553/how-chiefs-got-pressure-against-eagles-offensive-line)

- **Twists and stunts (T-E, E-T, knot stunts)** force adjacent linemen (often involving the center or a backup guard/tackle) to exchange rushers late in the down. Successful pass-off requires identical levels, hand placement, weight distribution, and verbal or visual cues honed through practice reps. With fewer than 50 career snaps together, the probability of a clean handoff drops sharply; one lineman “eats” the stunt while the other is left reaching or the rusher loops free. Baldinger’s breakdowns frequently show center/guard level mismatches or failed exchanges on exactly these looks. Thorn has highlighted tape of high-level interior linemen mastering “passing off & picking up the T-E stunt x 2” while also chipping mugged linebackers—implying the baseline expectation that most backups or new pairings cannot.[[6]](https://x.com/BrandonThornNFL/status/2117655331505328185)

- **A-gap mugged linebackers** and simulated pressures disrupt the center’s pre-snap rhythm and force guards or backs to account for immediate interior threats. This “mug” pins gaps, creates numbers advantages, or baits the slide the wrong way. Flores-style aggression and Spagnuolo’s overload concepts love these to isolate the running back or create free rushers in the B-gap.[[7]](https://www.matchquarters.com/p/jaguars-defense-campanile-fangio-flores)

- **Overload 5-0 fronts / load fronts** (five defenders on or near the line, often shifted or with extras in gaps) exploit half-slide or combo protections. They create voids between the slide and locked tackle, send multiple blitzers through the same gap, or pair a penetrating nose with a looping tackle (“knot” stunt). The offensive line must make rapid post-snap adjustments; a backup at guard or tackle with unfamiliar adjacent partners almost always loses these exchanges. Fangio, Spagnuolo, and similar schemers pair this with coverage rotations (fire zones, weak rotation, split-field) so the offense cannot simply check out of it.[[3]](https://x.com/The_Coach_A/status/2113992313160544675)[[4]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eoo6odNngdM)

These DCs do not wait for “average” performance to reveal itself. They attack the specific weak link or low-cohesion adjacent pair on early downs, forcing the offense into predictable slide directions or protection calls that can then be overloaded or twisted against.

### (2) Center Injury Breaks Pre-Snap MIKE Identification and Slide-Protection Calls Across the Entire Line

The center is the OL’s quarterback for identification and communication. He typically IDs the MIKE (the linebacker who sets strength or the primary threat for protection calls), makes the primary slide call (“slide left/right,” “I’m on you,” and higher-order terms), and coordinates the entire line’s assignments pre-snap. A backup center—or even a healthy center rattled by a mug or noise—can mis-ID the MIKE, call the wrong slide direction, or fail to communicate it clearly.[[8]](https://x.com/BaldyNFL/status/2109716172950094327)

When this happens, the ripple effects are immediate and line-wide:
- Guards and tackles slide the wrong way or pick up the wrong rusher on twists.
- The back or tight end chips the wrong gap.
- Everyone operates on mismatched assignments, turning a coordinated five-man wall into five individuals.

Baldinger has shown multiple examples where center/OG misalignment on basic double-A-gap or twist pressures leads to free rushers. Thorn’s evaluations emphasize how centers must process double mugs, titled noses, and stunts while still making accurate calls. An injury removes the practiced orchestrator; the new center lacks the shared language and anticipatory timing with the guards and tackles. The result is not a modest downgrade but systemic breakdown—precisely the non-linear penalty the “average of five linemen” model fails to capture.[[9]](https://x.com/BaldyNFL/status/1873913077927993410)

### (3) Mathematical Formulation of OL Pass Protection as Coupled Minimum-Operator + Ising/Potts Adjacency Interaction Tensor

A rigorous framing treats the OL (LT-LG-C-RG-RT plus any TE/RB chip help) as a one-dimensional chain with strong nearest-neighbor couplings. Overall protection success is dominated by a **minimum operator** across critical positions or paths (the weakest link determines failure; a single zero or near-zero blocks the play) rather than any average or sum.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJgFiFd_r34)

Add pairwise adjacency interactions that capture coordination chemistry. This maps naturally onto an **Ising/Potts-style model**:

- Each lineman *i* has a local “state” or performance variable *s_i* (e.g., blocking success probability, assignment correctness, or technique quality given the matchup).
- Local term: contribution ≈ min_i (skill_i(matchup, technique)) or a soft-min / bottleneck function. One low *s_i* collapses the pocket.
- Adjacency (coupling) term: for each neighboring pair (LG-C, C-RG, and higher-order terms), an interaction energy *J_{ij} · f(coord_{ij})* where *J_{ij}* scales with shared snaps, practice reps, and scheme familiarity. High *J* (veteran pair) favors aligned states (successful pass-off, matching levels, clean handoff on twists). Low *J* (backup + starter with <50 snaps) introduces a penalty—mismatch probability rises, like a frustrated or anti-ferromagnetic coupling.
- The full “Hamiltonian” or cost function for a protection configuration is something like:

  *E* = −∑_i local_blocking(*s_i*) + ∑_<ij> Penalty(1 − alignment_{ij}) + global_slide_call_error(Center_MIKE_ID)

  Protection integrity ~ exp(−*E*/temperature) or, more practically for evaluation, approximated by the minimum local term modulated by the product (or soft product) of adjacency success probabilities. A tensor formulation arises when considering the full configuration space of possible rusher assignments across the six positions; the adjacency tensor encodes allowed handoffs between neighbors.

In Potts generalization, each lineman can be in one of several discrete “blocking states” (e.g., which rusher they are responsible for post-snap). Adjacent linemen must agree on the boundary (pass-off); mismatch costs a large energy penalty. The center’s MIKE ID and slide call act as a global field that constrains the entire chain’s state space. Injuries or new pairings lower specific *J_{ij}*, dramatically increasing the probability of high-energy (failed) configurations even if average individual *s_i* looks acceptable.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJgFiFd_r34)

This model explains observed non-linearity: small drops in one link or one coupling strength produce disproportionate sack/pressure rate increases. It aligns with Thorn’s emphasis on infrastructure, cohesion, and scheme minimizing individual weaknesses; Baldinger’s film of communication breakdowns on twists and double-A pressures; and MatchQuarters-style schematic analysis of how Spagnuolo, Fangio, Flores *et al.* deliberately attack exactly these adjacency and identification vulnerabilities.[[2]](https://trenchwarfare.substack.com/p/how-offensive-structure-shapes-ol)

In short, OL evaluation and defensive attack plans treat the line as an entangled, coupled system whose performance is gated by its weakest link and its least-rehearsed adjacent pairs—not a simple average. The listed analysts’ film and data work repeatedly demonstrate this in practice.
